newsitem.title: USA: Viacom to name Blockbuster chief soon.
newsitem.headline: Viacom to name Blockbuster chief soon.

text.p: Viacom Inc Chairman Sumner Redstone said Thursday the company would soon name an executive to head its Blockbuster division.
"A new chairman will shortly be announced," Redstone said at the annual shareholders meeting here. He did not elaborate, and a spokeswoman had no other details.
Redstone acknowledged that problems had hampered operation at the video retailer, including high costs and purchasing of video tapes, but he said executives were working to fix the problems.

Redstone said that Wall Street was unfairly knocking down the price of Viacom stock because of the Blockbuster problems. He said that valuing shares at the current price -- 30-3/16, off 4/16 -- was "absurd and irrational."
He said one of his key objectives was to raise the share price, and he spent much of his presentation telling shareholders that virtually all of Viacom's businesses were doing well.

A stockholder asked whether Viacom intended to sell its 50 percent joint venture ownership in the USA Networks cable TV channel to partner Seagram Co Ltd's Universal Studios Inc unit. Redstone said Viacom was currently in discussions with Universal but did not give details.
A judge has ordered the two sides to work out a deal in which one side is likely to sell its stake to the other.
Late Wednesday Seagram said it was selling a chunk of its large holding in Time Warner Inc, and industry observers wonder whether Seagram will use the proceeds to get full control of USA.

Redstone said another one of his priorities is to continue to bring down the company's level of debt. He said he expects the debt to drop to a range of $6 billion to $8 billion by the year 2000 from $9.7 billion at the end of 1996. Redstone said debt would be reduced this year by $700 to $800 million from the sale of its radio stations business.
A shareholder resolution that would have required executives to publish contributions made to political campaigns or parties was soundly defeated.

But the shareholder who proposed the initiative, Evelyn Y. Davis, asked at the meeting for details on contributions. Philippe Dauman, deputy chairman, responded that a Viacom employee political action committee contributed $112,000 last year, about evenly split between the Democratic and Republican parties.

About a dozen members of the United Steelworkers of America demonstrated outside the meeting, accusing Viacom of refusing to clean up pollution at a Superfund site in Palmerton, Pa. The workers allege that the company has refused to clean up pollution at a former zinc mine, which has indirectly resulted in a loss of 100 jobs.
Viacom's involvement stems from its purchase of Paramount Communications, which was once known as Gulf and Western Industries Inc. Gulf and Western had once owned the mine.
Horsehead Resource Development Co Inc purchased the zinc operations from Gulf and Western in 1981.
Viacom said in a statement that it is currently in litigation with Horsehead over responsibility for the environmental cleanup.
"Horsehead is blaming Viacom for economic difficulties that resulted in layoffs, which we believe are in fact being caused by a dramamtic change in industry economics," Viacom said.
